en: Having prostrated before that God who is the mind-born one (*manobhava*), the all-pervading self of all, whose origin is known neither in the beginning nor in the middle, and by whom the entire world has been brought under his control; [I shall compose this treatise].
Prajāpati is indeed Manmatha himself, for without desire (kāma) there is no power for the procreation of beings;
and because that god is the self of all and omnipresent, he exists in both the great and the subtle.
Since there is nothing whatsoever beyond him, neither superior nor inferior, and since there is nothing other than him due to his subtlety and his greatness,
therefore this entire world is pervaded by that single Mind-born One, just as all is covered by the mountain Śṛṅgin.
May that Śambhu, who went to those who should not be approached, the Lord of Creatures, and Śakra whose body is marked with ten thousand women;
by whom the four-faced one was made and who is devoid of passion—may he bestow auspiciousness.
The Blessed One, who wields the Śārṅga bow and the mace,
attained the state of being "Blessed" (bhagavat) because he possesses many "blessings" (bhaga); thus the name "Bhagavān" was established for him, renowned throughout the world.
"Through separation from Sītā, Rāma, along with Lakṣmaṇa, underwent many sufferings;
recollecting those here in the Kali age, eight thousand and likewise eight [years] have been spent in marriage."
Those unfortunate women who are childless and sigh in distress, yet remain devoted to their husbands,
are constrained by the downfall of evil deities, and not by the very wicked deeds committed in other births.

Having gratified the best of the twice-born with the fragrances of sweet-smelling flowers on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable time and under a propitious constellation as prescribed by those who know the divine laws, one should give away one’s daughter while she is still in her prime— of pure descent on both sides, of known character, beautiful, and established in her youth.
On a day under the Puṣya asterism, or at an auspicious moment, or under the lunar mansions suitable for marriage,
one should have a well-proportioned image of Indrāṇī fashioned from clay by a skilled artisan.
Resplendent with garments and ornaments dyed with safflower, virtuous, beautiful, fortunate, and of noble birth, they—
having adorned the maiden together with the wife of Indra— should lead her to a river, a lake, or the riverbank.
Having offered a bali-oblation with a winnowing basket in the various directions, those women— smeared with fragrant *kālīyaka* paste,
their limbs wrapped in safflower-dyed garments— should lead the woman into the presence of Śacī.
Having worshipped the beloved of Śakra with curd-rice, oblation, and honey, and holding a piece of iron in her hand,
she should bow silently with her head to the Goddess and, joyful and with her hair restrained, go home while carrying the deity.
While that wife of Indra remains in the house, the maiden should worship her with garlands, perfumes, and incense during the morning, midday, and evening, until the time of her marriage arrives.
Jewels, moonbeams, garlands, auspicious dwellings, lotuses from palace rooftops,
fine liquors, betel, exquisite garments, charming songs,
and heaps of riches— indeed, for men, none of these lead to true delight without a woman.
Therefore, I shall speak that [grammar], which is the appropriate means for attaining it, and for the sake of dharma, artha, and kāma.
If the very same result that was stated regarding birth were to occur for women,
then this careful attention paid to the auspicious time, the lagna, and other factors at the moment of marriage would be in vain.
The primary factor is the unknown, while the secondary is that which manifests it in women;
in marriage, destiny leads [the woman] by its exceeding power, joined with the fruits of the [astrological] limits.
Vātsya desires that the year be unfavorable for conception; likewise, people desire what is superior to these.
The sages who were disciples of Māṇḍavya proclaimed the measurement of women's menses, excluding the *ṛtu* period. Parāśara, however, having rejected Caitra, declares it to bring misfortune to women.
Some twice-born sages have declared that [the period] beginning with Āṣāḍha and lasting for four months bestows auspicious results.
They dwell upon the most excellent fortnight, the bright one, as well as the first third of the dark fortnight;
likewise, having excluded the empty lunar days (riktā-tithi) and the junction of the two solstices, the remaining periods are auspicious.
On the days of the planets presided over by Agni (Agni, Bhauma, and Śukra), there is quarrel; however, on the auspicious days, there is excellent affection.
Some maintain that stability occurs on the day of the Sun, and on the day of the Moon, there is union with a wife.

A maiden wedded under Mṛgaśiras, Maghā, Hasta, Maitra (Anurādhā), the three Uttarās, Sva (Śravaṇa), Nairṛta (Mūla), Pūṣan (Puṣya), or Dhātṛ (Rohiṇī) gives birth to many sons and daughters, possesses female slaves and wealth, is endowed with good fortune, and brings satisfaction to her kinsmen.
In the four lunar mansions beginning with Ārdrā, widowhood is recorded; in those belonging to Agni and Yama (Kṛttikā and Bharaṇī), it is likewise remembered.
In the remaining [mansions], there is inexhaustible fault, grief, death, and much undesirable suffering such as disease.
In the case of the *tārakā* [planets] born under them, there is joy, and beyond that, results corresponding to their respective names;
and when the Moon is situated in the first or seventh house, there is the attainment of good fortune and happiness.
Garga stated that the fruit [of actions] performed during the *kṣaṇas* known as *nakṣatra-pas* is equal to that of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*).
Hārīta, Babhru, the twice-born Devala, and others declare that any other *karana*, with the exception of *viṣṭi*, is auspicious.

Parāśara has explained, in due order, the strength of the lunar day (*tithi*), the day (*dina*), the *karana*, the asterism (*rkṣa*), and the ascendant (*lagna*). Garga says that the lunar day is powerful; Bhāguri says that even the day is strong by virtue of the *karana*; Bhṛgu [says] it is by virtue of the day and *karana*; and Jīvaśarman declared the strength of the rising [ascendant] to be the power.
When there is equality [of the results], the karaṇas, lunar days, and asterisms that have been half-enjoyed do not produce their own fruits;
rather, the progression of the fourth parts (caraṇas) of the rising karaṇas, lunar days, and asterisms produces the results in succession.
In the sixth and eighth houses, there are the evils of death, enmity, and separation; in the second and twelfth, death; and in the trines (fifth and ninth), childlessness is declared.
In the seventh house, supreme affection is proclaimed; in the remaining positions, there is manifold happiness and the attainment of sons and wealth.
Even when there are six or eight [planets], one should observe the lord of the house itself as the dominant factor; having considered the single lordship and the sign of subjection (*vaśyarāśi*),
the time for marriage should be performed as auspiciously stated by the wise.
If the stars (tārā) should be mutually favorable to one another, it would be auspicious.
If the Moon is conjoined with the Sun, there is poverty; with Mars, death; with Mercury, one has no offspring;

with Jupiter, misfortune; and with Venus, one has a co-wife. Some maintain that if it is joined with Saturn or with the Moon and Jupiter, one enters the religious life (renunciation), yet they claim this results in auspiciousness.
Death occurs through diseases and various types of planetary afflictions; initiation and travels are auspicious when free from such obstacles.

In the third sign, Cancer, she whose mind is devoted to boys performs rites, she who is destitute of wealth observes the vow of a cow, she brings joy to two families, and she is an unchaste and cruel woman.
Born under Leo, she is devoted once to her father and is dear to her husband; under Virgo, she is excessively fond of her father-in-law.
Under Libra, she is intent on weighing and measuring things; likewise, under Scorpio, she is constantly weeping and unstable.
Others have declared that in Sagittarius she is unchaste, while in its first half she is a virtuous wife;
in Capricorn, Pisces, and Aquarius, she is incapable of other [sexual] acts and merely undergoes old age.
That portion which attains the state of a biped is auspicious when it rises in another house;
however, even within the houses of bipeds, other portions do not bring about auspiciousness.

From the asterism of the Sun's rising, it bestows death; then lack of great wealth; then acquisition of property from one's husband or heirs; then loss of wealth; then the destruction of kinsmen; then separation from sons; then great prosperity for the husband;
then widowhood; then not an early death; then loss of dharma; then immorality; and finally, it grants many gains as well as expenditure—in this sequence.

In the Śaśin yoga, there are horses and caravans; thereafter, one becomes beautiful, devoted to kinsmen and well-disposed, yet childless. A barren woman suffers from distress, while a woman with co-wives faces the death of her husband.

Then, in the Janitrī yoga, there are daughters, and one’s undertakings are frustrated. Some say she becomes extremely wealthy but incapable of expenditure; others declare this yoga brings ill fortune to kinsmen and ends in water.

Death, poverty, hostility toward one's caravan, enmity with kinsmen, lack of sons, and discord with one's husband do not occur; however, when Mars is in the *anukūla* yoga, there is the discharge of blood, cruelty like that of a flesh-eating beast, and the destruction of one's own kin.

In the Saumya (Mercury) house, one becomes devoted to her husband, a virtuous housewife, honored by her husband’s kin, revered by her relatives, and blessed with many sons; she conquers her enemies, yet may be barren, lifeless, emaciated by religious observances and charity, deceitful, wealthy, and prone to expenditure.
When Jupiter is in the seventh house, the wife is dear to her husband, very wealthy, joyful, blessed with fortune and riches, endowed with sons, and she does not disagree with her husband;
she is long-lived, devoted to auspicious things, successful in her undertakings, possessed of her own property, and beneficial to both [her husband and herself].

She is beloved by her husband, yet greedy; she is capable through innate power over her husband, yet devoted to the welfare of her family. She possesses excellent sons, yet is full of enmity; thereafter, she becomes unchaste and meets an early death. [But] she who is always delighted in dharma and takes pleasure in manifold virtuous deeds— VP_37a/.priyā patyur lubdhā patisahajaśaktā kulahitā VP_37b/.suputrā vairāḍhyā tad anu kulaṭā kṣipranidhanā/ VP_37c/.ratā nityaṃ dharme bahukuśalakarmaṇy abhiratā/ VP_37d/.sā bhartuḥ priyā syāt sarvaguṇasampannā caiva bhavati// VP_38// She is dear to her husband, yet covetous; she is endowed with innate power over her husband and is beneficial to her kin. She has good sons, yet is rich in hostility; subsequently, she becomes wanton and dies quickly. However, she who is constantly intent on dharma and delights in many wholesome actions—she shall be dear to her husband and indeed become perfected in all virtues. // VP_38 //
"It becomes one where income predominates and where wealth has been exhausted," so it was said by Bhṛgu.
If the Sun is in the seventh house, the woman will be unchaste, possess great wealth, and yield little milk;
she will suffer from heart disease, be overcome by her enemies, and be prone to miscarriages.
Freed from diseases, yet having lapsed from her vows and being of sinful character and excessively wealthy,
she gradually brings her riches to ruin through drinking, once she has become deeply attached.
Venus, having left the fourth, twelfth, seventh, eighth, third, sixth, and first houses, is auspicious; the Moon, situated in the third, second, eleventh, or fifth house, is likewise auspicious.

Malefic planets, having left the eighth house, are beneficial for marriage when situated in the third, sixth, eighth, or eleventh house; however, Mars, even if leaving the eighth house, does not grant desirable results.
If Jupiter or Venus is situated in the fifth, fourth, tenth, first,
or ninth house, whatever inauspiciousness approaches turns into auspiciousness, and even that which is auspicious attains further increase through their power.
Even when situated in an unfavorable position, the Moon bestows praiseworthy results if it is aspected by a strong Mercury that is its own friend or a great friend.
When the strength of the human planets (the Sun, Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Venus) prevails, a woman has a husband who is her beloved;
when the opposite is the case, she becomes the mistress of her husband, or one might infer other consequences from this principle.
If Venus, the Sun, or Saturn are combust, or if they are situated in an inimical sign or its navāṃśa,
a woman quickly falls into conflict with her mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband due to delusion.

If the ascendant degree is not aspected by its own lord at the time of marriage, there will be the destruction of the man; likewise, if it is so for the seventh house degree, there will be the destruction of the woman.
If either Jupiter or Venus is in its exaltation and situated in the ascendant, a maiden is born;
she will undoubtedly become a queen if both Jupiter and Mercury are so placed.

When the ascendant is a benefic sign and there is the rising of one's own or a friendly planet, the *caturthikā* rite should be performed. Lovers resembling one's own caste [are indicated] by three or more planets situated in a single asterism.
The virtuous [author] spoke of the moon, which bestows auspiciousness in marriage, as being situated in the sign of Cancer;
however, that contradicts the words of the Sage, for it was not stated in the Sūtra regarding the wind-constellation (Svāti) and the Vaiśvadeva-constellation (Jyeṣṭhā).
Marriages joined within the wheel of the twelve zodiac signs at the time of the rising of the signs have been prescribed by the sages.
Śrī Devakīrti, listen to the Āryā verses concerning the names [of the signs] in that wheel, the planetary conjunctions, and the ascendant.
Nanda, Bhadra, Jīva, Jīmūta, Sthāvara, Jaya, Vijaya, Vyāla,
Rasātalamukha, Kṣaya, and Tama are the final group [of yogatārās] used for marriage.
When the Moon is in the ascendant, it is Nanda; likewise, when Venus is there, it is Bhadra, and when Jupiter, it is Jīva.
With the first and last [planets], it is Jīmūta; with the middle and last, it is Sthāvara.
Furthermore, by those [planets] being gentle—namely the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—or by the Sun, Mars, and Saturn, respectively:
it should be known that [a yoga] with gentle planets is gentle, while those declared [to be] with cruel planets are cruel.
Through conjunction with the Sun, Vyāla; with Mars, Rasātala; with Saturn, Kṣaya;
with Rāhu (Tamas), Tama is declared; and finally, through Ketu, Kṛtānta.
Among the three [houses] beginning with Nandā, she is a queen; from the fourth onwards, she is a great queen.
Among the five beginning with Vyāla, she is a widow, pitiable, and poor.
One who is not authorized by these [planets] may be a doer of merit; otherwise, the Moon is authorized by them.
Therefore, at the time of marriage, the Moon is auspicious when it is not conjoined with anything [else].

Those seven lunar yogas of yours, when joined with the benefics, bring about the accomplishment of all undertakings; however, when joined with the malefics, they yield inauspicious results and must be avoided at the time of marriage.
Therefore, having reflected upon these methods, a wise person should apply them in all undertakings.
When Nanda’s daughter has been wed, she shall soon attain the title of Queen.

O auspicious lady, if at the time of taking the hand in marriage a young maiden approaches [the altar], she becomes beloved by her husband even more than his own life, and becomes the mother of a ruler of men.
But she, being swift, brings the title of "king" to her husband and also to his lineage.
A maiden married under the asterism called Jyeshtha is proclaimed to bring victory to her husband.
She attains the threefold aims of life and gladdens both families;
having been wedded by Jīmūta, she enjoys vast and highly fruitful pleasures.
Having seen his grandson and son together with their wives attain divinity,
and having entered into a marriage alliance with a maiden born of a *sthāvara-yoga*, he shall obtain vast sovereignty.

By obtaining the treasure of her husband, she brings about the elevation of her family; by attaining the taking of his hand in marriage, even one born of a lowly family gains the sovereignty of her husband.
A maiden who is constantly attended by her co-wives always brings prosperity;
having attained marriage through Vijayā, she obtains sons, fame, and the acquisition of wealth.
By destiny, a girl who is like a serpent approaches the hand-grasping ceremony at the hands of a serpent-like man, for the sake of the lineage's stability and the celestial realm after death.
Afflicted by poverty and disease, she does not take pleasure in any one man;
having entered that which is called the underworld at the time of marriage, she remains there for five months.
Having incurred that incomparable fault, the other [the husband] gives up his life;
having reached ruin through marriage, the maiden kills her husband from both sides.
But with a low-born husband, she consumes her lineage through the fire of her paramour;
even if she is endowed with auspicious marks, virtues, and wealth, she does so if her marriage was contracted in secret.
Even if she has been born by the Lord of the Gods, he consumes her after seventy nights;
yet, if by fate the maiden reaches marriage through the conjunction of destiny, [she survives].
She destroys the circle of her father-in-law’s kinsmen in a short time;
thus, by implication, the categories of those who neglect themselves, those who nourish them, and those who kill them have been stated.
From these [planets], one should indicate whether the result is auspicious or inauspicious by means of the birth ascendant and the lord of the birth ascendant.
The birth ascendant is proclaimed as the "self" (ātman), and from that, the fifth and ninth houses are likewise designated.
The tenth house, consisting of twelve signs, is designated as being called "indifferent" (*upekṣaka*).
The eleventh house is to be known as difficult to accomplish, related to the wife, and nourishing.
The twelfth *nidhana* (concluding section), the fourth, is designated in the treatise as "the Slayer" (*vadhaka*).
If, excluding the Moon, there are seven benefics and five malefics, why is it not called "the Seven"? (VP 71ab)
Why was it not stated that one hundred multiplied by three (three hundred) should be subtracted from the ascendant for the conjunctions of two, three, and so on?
First, the local custom must be considered; in every region, whatever the established practice may be, that alone should be followed.
The wise avoid that which is hated by the world; even an astrologer should proceed according to the ways of the world.

The Southerners desire marriage when Jupiter is situated in an auspicious *gocara*, while the Gauḍas say it is when the Sun is in an auspicious position. In Mālava, the *gocara* is not considered authoritative.
When Hari is asleep, during the southern solstice, in the month of Caitra, or under the asterism named Puṣya;
on an inauspicious lunar day (riktā), when the moon has waned, or on the days of the Sun, Moon, Mars, and Saturn—it is inauspicious.
Three days struck by Vyatīpāta are equal to Vyatīpāta itself, as is Vaidhṛti.
Even that [calculation] is doubled when a clear eclipse is observed, or else it is not certain;
Vyatīpāta and Vyāghāta occur in the sixth lunar mansion, and Vaidhṛta occurs in the tenth.
*Vikṣobhaṇa*, *gaṇḍānta*, and the conjunctions known as *atidhṛti* and *vyāghāta*;
those people situated in the northern direction call this *vyatipāta*.
Like the *vyatipāta* yoga, it remains agitated amidst the causes for the distinctions of many philosophical systems;
likewise, the northern regions, adjacent to Sākala, extend over the two and a half [units] of the Māṇḍavya region.
In Khaśa, Hūṇa, or Bāhlīka, nor in the regions of Kānada, nor among the Gopas and Bhojas—
these eleven asterisms are declared auspicious; the remaining ones are unfavorable at the time of marriage.

In that case, the star Agni, conjoined with the potency of the Moon, and the thirty *muhūrtas* should be considered. In a marriage *lagna* arising from Libra, Virgo, or Gemini, the one situated there yields evil results, and no others do.
In a month, one should consider the divisions of the thirty-part [signs] and the twelve-part [signs], beginning with the decans (dreṣkāṇa) and the horās;
furthermore, there are eight lunar mansions in a month that are defective due to the Viṣṭi yoga, and regarding these, some say they include both night and day.

The attainment and destruction of *viṣṭi* occur at the end of the half-tithi; the lunar measure is the cause of *viṣṭi*, not the remainder. The Easterners, for the most part, say that the time of twilight—along with the cows and those of inferior caste—is the desired [time], not the remainder.
As long as the dust raised by the cows has not subsided, so long shall there be purity of mind for them at the wedding.

When the dust raised at the end of day by the hooves of cows struck by the herders' sticks settles during the marriage of beautiful women, there will be abundant wealth, sons, longevity, and the perfection of health.

At that time, neither the lunar mansion, nor the lunar day, nor the *karana*, nor the ascendant, nor the planetary conjunction is required for the sake of men’s happiness; indeed, the dust raised by a cow pacifies all misfortunes. Furthermore, the mental disposition of a family or a region should never be subjected to fragmentation by a wise man.
Whatever fault might be imagined here against the astrologer even on account of his being a physician, that is attributed by the ignorant;
for although they speak in many ways without understanding the body of the treatise, it is not [our] approval.
For those who follow Kaṇāda, the wise man should close his eyes when the [planet] has entered its domain;
likewise at the time of marriage, departure, or entry, or during other auspicious rites.
Those of sharp intellect who, being poorly trained astrologers, proclaim a fault based on passion—homage be to them!
And the *Tigmakiraṇa* [yoga] is for a man; marriage may also take place with those remaining asterisms.
A complete endowment of all auspicious qualities is not obtained in a few days; therefore, one should join [the bride] with many excellent qualities during the auspicious rites.
Indeed, a multitude of virtues does not give rise to a fault, just as a mere drop of water cannot extinguish a fire with well-kindled fuel.

Even a hundred virtues may be destroyed by a single fault that has grown large, provided there is no other opposing virtue present. A single drop of wine, by its power, defiles even an entire jar filled to the brim with the five products of the cow.
Having performed the auspicious rites of the marriage-thread ceremony, the bridegroom, immediately after partaking of the honey-mixture and other foods, [proceeds].
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious result one obtains from a fire that blazes like a flaming fire, he attains that very same [result].
Having prostrated before the virtuous, Varāhamihira has composed this *Vivāhapaṭala*, omitting its excessive length from the *Cakra*.
Furthermore, having reflected upon what was previously stated by me regarding the rite for the birth of a young woman, that should be considered with discernment as to what is true and what is false.
The end of the Vivāhapāṭala.
